Experiments on synthetic and eBay data show gains from exploiting MHR and the benefits of the robust rule when parametric models are misspecified.
comment: 87 pages, 12 figures, 25 tables. Authors listed alphabetically

title: Fluidic Body: Swarm Robots as a Fluid Extension of the Hand
comments: accepted to ACM ISS 2026 (ISS track of PACMHCI)
summary: Swarm robots have attracted growing interest as a physical interface for human--computer interaction, since a swarm can reshape its formation to fit the objects and surroundings it works with. For a human operator, however, adapting the swarm's behavior remains difficult. Most existing methods require the user to specify where the swarm should go, and they offer no intuitive way to change the collective's behavior as each task demands. We present Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand. The system places a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm, and the user adapts the swarm's behavior to each task by changing the fluid's properties through simple hand movements. When the user opens the hand, the swarm becomes soft enough to deform and flow around obstacles. Closing the hand turns it into a hard, cohesive body that can push objects. We evaluated the controller's performance and its operability in two simulation experiments and one demonstration with physical robots. First, our controller handled both obstacle avoidance and object transportation better than an existing method that behaves the same way in every task. Second, in a VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with that method. They also reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency. Finally, this experience carried over to physical robots in a real-world demonstration (88 participants). These results suggest that treating a swarm as a fluid, a material people already understand, allows a robot swarm to work as a deformable extension of the human body.
comment: accepted to ACM ISS 2026 (ISS track of PACMHCI)

title: SynMOE: A Syntax-Aware MOE-Guided Approach for PEFT-Based Code Intelligence Learning
summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as an important approach for adapting Language Models (LMs) in downstream tasks. However, in the domain of code intelligence, the performance of most PEFT methods relatively drops compared to Full fine-Tuning (FT), hindering their broader applicability. One of the main reasons is that current PEFT methods are generally based on assumptions about the low-rank nature or sparsity of parameter updates, lacking explicit modeling of code-related information. To tackle this limitation, we propose SynMOE, a syntax-aware MOE-guided approach for PEFT on code intelligence learning. Specifically, SynMOE contains two stages: syntactic information extraction and syntax-aware MOE-guided adaptation. It first obtains the syntactic labels of source code from Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), and then aligns the labels with the input tokens of code LMs. In the second stage, syntactic labels are integrated into the MOE module, participating in the routing decision of MOE for a more powerful syntactic-aware token representation. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach by applying it to two typical PEFT methods, LoRA and $(IA)^3$, across three diverse code intelligence tasks. Experimental results show that SynMOE achieves consistent and significant improvements. Even compared to FT, SynMOE achieves comparable or superior performance while being more computationally efficient. In addition, we also conduct ablation studies, hyperparameter analysis, and evaluation in the low-resource scenario to provide a comprehensive investigation of the proposed approach.

title: RouTex: Multi-reference 3D Texture Generation by Reprogramming Rotary Position Encoding
summary: While single-image 3D texture generation has advanced significantly, conditioning texture synthesis on multi-view reference images remains largely under-explored, despite its necessity for resolving surface ambiguity in unobserved regions. In this paper, we propose RouTex, a novel multi-reference 3D texture generation framework based on in-context Diffusion Transformers (DiT). Our key insight is that native 3D Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) inherently possesses spatial addressing capabilities. We introduce Positional Routing (PR) to reprogram 3D RoPE along spatial and semantic dimensions, establishing explicit reference-to-view correspondence without introducing additional parameters. To execute this routing efficiently, Dual-Granularity Attention (DGA) combines per-view local attention for fine texture fidelity with global joint attention over deduplicated references for cross-view consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RouTex achieves new state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.

title: File-Semantic SSD for I/O-centric Architectures with NFS-over-NVMe Protocol
summary: Emerging I/O-centric architectures empower peripheral devices to access storage directly while bypassing the host CPU and kernel. However, SSDs expose only a block interface and rely on the host filesystem for file metadata and access control, making file-level access for applications and peripheral devices inherently difficult in I/O-centric architectures. This tight coupling between the host filesystem and storage device introduces unavoidable software overhead and limits the potential of fully hostless I/O paths. In this paper, we present File-Semantic SSD (FS-SSD), a new SSD architecture that provides a native file abstraction within SSDs, enabling direct file access by peripheral and remote devices without host intervention. FS-SSD adopts the lightweight, stateless NFS interface and introduces NFS-over-NVMe, a protocol extension that embeds NFS operations into the standard NVMe command structure. This allows FS-SSD to support local and remote file I/O through existing PCIe and NVMe-oF transports. Our evaluation shows that FS-SSD provides on-device file abstraction while fully utilizing raw-device bandwidth in I/O-centric architectures.

title: Which One Is Sounding? Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation
summary: Existing audio-visual segmentation methods mainly predict sound-related regions or category masks and often fail to identify the sounding instance when multiple same-class candidates coexist. Recent audio-visual instance segmentation methods address instance-level prediction but rely largely on motion and cross-frame association, which may become unreliable under sparse observations or inconspicuous motion. To this end, we introduce binaural audio, whose interaural differences encode source-direction information, to provide spatial constraints for distinguishing the sounding instance among same-class visual candidates. We propose Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation (BiSID-AVS), which progressively refines category-level candidate responses into a mask of the true sounding instance. BiSID-AVS first grounds category-consistent candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial response map, and finally refines the true sounding instance through dual-level spatial conditioning at the feature and decoder levels. Experiments on the binaurally extended AVS-Synthetic benchmark and Habitat-AVS dataset for robotic indoor perception show that BiSID-AVS achieves the best performance on the multi-candidate subsets, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points, respectively, while substantially reducing false activation on non-sounding same-class regions.

title: UniCompress: From Multi-LoRA Experts to One Compact Model for Edge Intelligence
summary: Embodied and edge systems increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to support heterogeneous skills, yet deploying a separate task adapter for each skill while retaining a high-precision backbone creates substantial memory and management costs. We present UniCompress, a deployment-oriented framework that converts multi-task expertise into one compact, adapter-free model. Starting from a consolidated BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher, UniCompress constructs an asymmetric INT2 student using GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery. The approach jointly quantizes and recovers the projection weights in the vision encoder and language backbone, enabling aggressive compression of the complete vision-language model while preserving its multi-task behavior. We evaluate UniCompress on four heterogeneous embodied tasks: posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing, and mobile-GUI action prediction. UniCompress reduces the approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB in BF16 to 2.1 GB in INT2, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 76%. It improves the INT2 macro task score by 34.3 percentage points over GPTQ-INT2 while remaining within 0.9 points of the consolidated BF16 teacher. These results demonstrate the potential of teacher-guided joint vision-language INT2 recovery for deploying a single multi-skill VLM on resource-constrained embodied platforms.

title: Breaking the One-Player Extension Barrier: History-Aware Repair for Multiplayer Approximate Nash Equilibria
summary: Computation of Nash equilibria is a central problem in algorithmic game theory, yet exact equilibrium computation is $\mathsf{PPAD}$-complete even for two-player games. This hardness motivates the study of polynomial-time algorithms for approximate Nash equilibria. While substantial progress has been made for two-player and three-player games, existing algorithms for general $m$-player games have largely relied on repeatedly applying one-player extension starting from improved fixed-player algorithms. Such improvements can at best strengthen the classical $1-1/m$ guarantee to $1-1/(m-c)$, for some constant $c$ independent of $m$. We break this long-standing barrier by developing an iterative algorithm that directly tackles general $m$-player games and achieves a $(1-(σ_{\star}-ε)/m)$-approximation for fixed $ε> 0$ and sufficiently large $m$, where $σ_\star\approx1.5867$ is the unique root in $(1,2)$ of $σ_\star^3-19σ_\star^2+27σ_\star+1=0$. Our approach rests on a novel iterative descent-and-repair framework that allows multiple rounds of repair. At the heart of our analysis is a new potential function inspired by continuous-time dynamics, which certifies progress across iterations and ensures polynomial-time termination. Our results highlight the power of history-aware, iterative repair in breaking approximation barriers for multiplayer games.

title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts
comments: SysPilot is open source at https://github.com/yinengy/SysPilot
summary:
Modern scientific and machine-learning applications compose many independently developed libraries. When these libraries run together, their independently managed runtimes can oversubscribe shared resources: using the same CPU cores, fighting over GPUs, or contending for memory bandwidth. Avoiding such contention requires careful configuration across library boundaries. Existing autotuners do not directly investigate what resources are shared between libraries, which runtime signals correlate with interference. As a result, they are inefficient for finding optimal configurations to mitigate contention.
  This paper presents SysPilot, a cross-library performance autotuning system based on Library Performance Contract (LPC). A Library Performance Contract captures a library's resource demands, assumptions, controls, and observability signals in LPCL, a specification language for describing library resource requirements. SysPilot synthesizes contracts from documentation and code artifacts, composes contracts from the libraries used by an application, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the application to validate those hypotheses, and selects candidate configurations. This design makes the Library Performance Contract a reusable unit of performance knowledge: a contract for a library can be reused across many applications that depend on that library. We evaluate SysPilot on a benchmark suite of cross-library contention scenarios. The results show that SysPilot matches the performance of autotuners that rely on application-specific manual information while retaining cross-application reuse. Compared with general-purpose autotuners such as OpenTuner and SMAC3, SysPilot improves benchmark performance metrics by up to an additional 38% over the best configuration found by these autotuners, while using 3x fewer runs.
comment: SysPilot is open source at https://github.com/yinengy/SysPilot

title: TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
summary: Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq's Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware schedulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condition for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code structure. We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The programmer schedules operations, loops, and composed kernels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring schedules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR, its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear program, using explicit times to group connected operations into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycleaccurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves a $1.40\times$ latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cycle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636 GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at 32.

title: Catastrophic Overfitting is Weight Drift the Training Loss Cannot See
comments: 12 pages (including appendix), 7 figures, 6 tables. Code available at https://github.com/fzjcdt/co-weight-drift
summary: Fast adversarial training (FAT) makes robust training affordable by replacing the multi-step attack with a single-step one, but it suffers from catastrophic overfitting (CO): partway through training, robustness to multi-step attacks collapses to near zero while the single-step attack used for training keeps being repelled. We show that CO is a quiet escape of the weights. Across the event the network's clean behavior quietly improves, and moving from the weights just before CO to those just after it changes the training objective only marginally while destroying most of the robustness. The training objective is therefore nearly blind to the displacement it causes, so it exerts no force to undo it. The exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights, which FAT protocols already maintain, does not accumulate this drift and stays robust through the entire event. This observation suggests a nearly free fix: when validation robustness drops, reset the weights to their EMA. We build this guard on top of a coupling-based base method designed so that its average stays inside the robust region. The resulting training removes CO in every one of our runs and attains the strongest AutoAttack accuracy among fast methods on all three benchmark datasets, including a clear margin on CIFAR-100, where it also clears the multi-step reference at roughly half its cost. Code is available at https://github.com/fzjcdt/co-weight-drift.
comment: 12 pages (including appendix), 7 figures, 6 tables. Code available at https://github.com/fzjcdt/co-weight-drift

title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?
summary: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8%}; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.

title: Shallow Encoding Emits Deep Memories
comments: 47 pages. Mingyuan Ma and Yangmin Li contributed equally
summary: Hybrid language models interleave a few softmax-attention layers with many linear-attention or state-space layers, so every layer keeps a memory of earlier tokens: a key-value cache or a fixed-size recurrent state. Serving them spends more compute and high-bandwidth memory on these memories than the output requires. The prefill runs every layer for every prompt token, and every decode step loads and stores whole recurrent states, which on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next take as many bytes per request as the attention cache of thousands of tokens. We find two properties of trained hybrids that locate this excess. First, writes are easier than reads: writing a deep layer's memory of a token needs little of the deep computation that predicting the next token needs. Trained copies of the deep layers' write paths, which we call emitters, therefore write a prompt's deep memories from the residual stream of a shallower anchor layer, and all prompt tokens but the last run as few as 63% of the layers. Second, recurrent states have a state sink: most of their energy lies in a rank-one term along a fixed direction of each head, and the rest is a low-rank working memory. SEED builds on both: it makes the prefill shallow in depth and the decode state shallow in representation. Each recurrent state is stored as its sink plus low-rank factors, which the Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention and Mamba-2 updates extend exactly; we prove that the open-loop error of the periodic compressions back to low rank is bounded independently of their number. SEED keeps the original weights frozen, compresses no attention cache, and runs all layers for every generated token. On six checkpoints of five production hybrids of 30B to over 300B parameters, it is nearly lossless on eleven official exams. Served with SGLang on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs on an agentic-coding trace, it raises the per-GPU throughput of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 1.2-1.4x.
comment: 47 pages. Mingyuan Ma and Yangmin Li contributed equally

title: GeoBiaset: A Counterfactual Benchmark for Demographic Bias in World-Level Geolocalization
comments: Accepted at Neurips 2026, E&D track. Project page: https://miccunifi.github.io/GeoBiaset/
summary: World-level image geolocalization is an increasingly important task, yet the biases of current models remain poorly understood. Prior work has identified coarse dataset imbalances noting, for instance, that some cities are absent from training sets and that models tend to perform better in wealthier regions. However, no one has yet examined which visual cues drive these disparities. To do so, we introduce GeoBiaset, the first benchmark designed to measure how geolocalization models are influenced by the apparent race of a person inserted into the image foreground. The dataset consists of 9,541 images, pairing existing geotagged background images with counterfactual edits spanning seven races, holding the ground-truth coordinates fixed. Controlled masking experiments show that occlusion and background drift do not fully explain geolocalization degradation. Alongside the benchmark, we introduce the Person-Origin Perturbation Indicators (POPI), novel metrics that quantify model resilience to these demographic perturbations by measuring whether predictions are pulled toward the region associated with the inserted group. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art geolocalization and multimodal large language models reveals a 16-47% drop in continent-level performance when a subject from a demographically mismatched group is inserted. A landmark versus no-landmark analysis and gradient-weighted heatmaps show that models preferentially attend to geographic landmarks when present, but shift attention to facial features in their absence.
comment: Accepted at Neurips 2026, E&D track. Project page: https://miccunifi.github.io/GeoBiaset/

title: STARE: Scene Text-Aware multimodal Retrieval for Everyday objects
summary: In this study, we focus on service robots that retrieve and transport everyday objects based on free-form instructions that may refer to visual features and scene text. This is challenging because it requires a multimodal understanding of the visual features and spatial relationships of objects, as well as scene text embedded in the environment. To address this, we propose Scene Text-Aware multimodal Retrieval for Everyday objects (STARE), which leverages visual and textual cues in response to free-form instructions. STARE introduces Crosslingual Visual Prompt to enhance scene text interpretation, and models the complex relationships between named entities in the instructions and their corresponding objects. We evaluate STARE using two novel benchmarks, GoGetIt and TextCaps-test, both of which consist of real-world indoor/outdoor images and instructions involving object manipulation and navigation. The results show that STARE outperforms all baseline methods on standard multimodal retrieval metrics. Furthermore, in physical experiments conducted under a zero-shot transfer setting, STARE achieves an overall success rate of 80%. Our project page and code are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

title: Overview of the NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval Task: Cross-modal Claim Verification in Scientific Papers
comments: The first two authors contributed equally. More information about the shared task is available at https://sciclaimeval.github.io/
summary: This paper presents an overview of \emph{SciClaimEval}, a pilot task at NTCIR-19 on verifying scientific claims against the tables and figures of the papers in which they appear. Our dataset pairs authentic claims from 180 papers in machine learning, natural language processing, and medicine with contrastive versions of their tables and figures, one supporting the claim and one minimally modified so that it does not. The task comprises two subtasks: deciding whether a piece of evidence supports a claim, and selecting which of two evidence versions does. Twenty-two teams registered, the highest number among NTCIR-19 tasks, and 14 submitted 177 runs. Most systems built on multimodal large language models, relying on prompting and multi-stage inference rather than task-specific fine-tuning. On the first subtask, the best systems reached 98.1\% pair accuracy, but all six top-ranked systems relied on the contrastive pairs; the best system that judged each claim-evidence pair on its own scored 24.3 points lower. Open-weight models, embedded in carefully designed pipelines, matched proprietary ones. Yet verifying a single claim against its evidence, the setting that matters in practice, remains an open problem.
comment: The first two authors contributed equally. More information about the shared task is available at https://sciclaimeval.github.io/

title: Constant-Round Massively Parallel Algorithms for Approximate MSTs in Metric Spaces
summary:
We develop a unified algorithmic framework for computing approximate minimum spanning trees (MSTs) in metric spaces in the fully scalable Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Using this framework, we obtain the following results for any fixed constant $σ\in(0,1)$:
  - General metrics: Given all pairwise distances, we compute a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate MST in $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ rounds using $n^σ$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ total space.
  - Euclidean spaces: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we compute an $O(1/σ^4)$-approximate MST in $O(1)$ rounds using $(nd)^σ$ local space per machine and $O(nd+n^{1+σ})$ total space.
  - Doubling metrics: Given $n$ points in a metric of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}=O(σ\log n)$, we compute an $O(1/σ)$-approximate MST in $O(\mathrm{ddim}/σ^4)$ rounds using $n^σ$ local space per machine and $\widetilde{O}(n^{1+σ})\cdot 2^{O(\mathrm{ddim})}$ total space.
  For any fixed constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, these results give the first constant-round MPC algorithms achieving $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation in general metrics and $O(1)$-approximation in a high-dimensional Euclidean space, respectively. They improve upon the $O(\log\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))$-round algorithm for general metrics [SODA'25] and the $O(\log\log n\cdot\log\log\log n)$-round algorithm for Euclidean spaces [SODA'24], respectively. Moreover, our round complexity for general metrics is asymptotically optimal in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, matching the $Ω(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ lower bound of [SODA'25] under the 1-vs-2-cycles conjecture. Our result also answers an open question raised by [STOC'23].

title: Drift-adaptive Representation Preservation for Domain-Incremental Learning
summary: Pretrained vision models provide strong general-purpose representations, but in Domain-Incremental Learning (DIL), where the input distribution changes sequentially, adapting to new domains often degrades performance on previously learned ones. We observe that forgetting is not uniform across domains and classes and is not explained by training order alone. This motivates us to track each past domain-class concept individually. We use representation drift, defined as the deviation of a past concept's current representation from a fixed anchor, as a measurable surrogate for forgetting risk. The measured drift then serves two complementary roles. A consolidation loss assigns stronger preservation to high-drift pairs, while prototype construction down-weights highly drifted domains to reduce their influence on the class reference. Preservation is thus allocated by measured drift rather than assumed importance. To obtain this signal during training without storing past raw data, we repurpose a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). For each domain-class pair, we store only a compact context summary in the backbone feature space and rerun it through the learned context-to-target relation to measure its drift from the fixed anchor. Across DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50, and CDDB-Hard, our method sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on every benchmark, using substantially less training memory than accuracy-competitive methods and the smallest storage among compared methods.

title: Reasoning-Trace Overflow in Code Generation: An Empirical Study of Explicit Reasoning Models
summary: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.

title: Many Pixels, One Composition: Self-Supervised Spectra for Specimen-Level Prediction
summary: Can hyperspectral (HS) imaging be used to predict the elemental composition of physical specimens found on the Earth's surface? We approach this problem as a supervised regression task, using an open dataset of specimens, each comprising a HS cube and elemental characterization. In particular, we train an encoder in a self-supervised fashion that operates on pixel-level; then freeze the encoder and train a lightweight attention-based regression head in a supervised manner, by pairing many representations of a given specimen with its corresponding elemental label. In test specimens, our approach significantly outperforms traditional spectral matching and unmixing baselines. It also outperforms supervised learning models based on the mean spectrum (of similar model capacity), while full model fine-tuning achieves the strongest performance, at substantially higher model capacity.

title: Two-Sided Screening in Quality-Differentiated Markets
summary:
Motivated by digital marketplaces such as Uber and Airbnb, we study how a two-sided platform designs a menu of qualities, consumer prices, and provider wages. Consumers and providers self-select according to their private values and costs, so the platform must design its menu to attract consumers while inducing enough supply to meet their demand. We study this coordination problem over a continuous quality space, requiring supply to cover demand at every quality threshold.
  We formulate menu design as an optimization over trading distributions, which specify how much trade occurs at or above each quality. Through convexification of the technological cost function, we characterize the profit- and welfare-optimal trading distributions. This characterization shows how production technology alone can reduce menu size without sacrificing optimal profit or welfare, regardless of the type distributions, and determines when optimal menus can be finite. We then show that profit maximization can be highly efficient: under monotone hazard rate conditions on both sides, a profit-optimal menu achieves at least $1/(e-1)$ of optimal social welfare.
  We next consider the practical setting in which the menu size is restricted to a prescribed number of offers. We establish how the restricted menu approximates the unrestricted optimum in profit. We develop an algorithm that computes a menu within this size limit in polynomial time. The computed menu simultaneously approximates the unrestricted optimal profit and social welfare with additive error.

title: Towards Insight-Centric Data Spaces: Integrating Visual Analytics and Decentralized Data Ecosystems
summary: Visual analytics and dataspaces address complementary challenges in modern data ecosystems: visual analytics enables interactive exploration and human-centered reasoning over complex data, dataspaces provide decentralized infrastructures for sovereign and collaborative data sharing. Both fields have largely evolved independently, resulting in a gap between data management and data understanding in distributed environments.We explore their intersection and argue that integration is essential for next-generation data ecosystems. Visual analytics acts as a cognitive layer for dataspaces by making data availability, quality, provenance, and exchange processes observable and interpretable, while dataspaces reshape visual analytics by introducing decentralized, heterogeneous, and governed data environments. We illustrate this interplay through a semi-synthetic cultural dataspace scenario analyzing exchange patterns and metadata quality across a federated ecosystem. Based on these insights, we identify key open challenges and outline a vision of insight-centric data spaces, in which data management and analysis are tightly integrated into a unified, human-centered environment.

title: SWEOps-Bench: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Resolution of Software-Induced Cloud Incidents
summary:
As autonomous agents advance, the traditional boundary between software development and cloud operations gradually blurs, increasing the need for integrated incident detection, localization, and remediation. Existing benchmarks evaluate isolated diagnostic queries or repository-level program repair, failing to test continuous incident resolution across operational clusters and source repositories. We introduce SWEOps-Bench, an interactive benchmark comprising 55 reproducible incident tasks derived from confirmed historical defects across 16 Kubernetes operator projects. Each task preserves the original software repository and initializes in a healthy cluster before a controlled workload triggers the historical fault. Agents investigate runtime evidence and submit source or configuration repairs through a terminal interface, while the harness builds and deploys the changes within a shared time budget.
  Evaluation covers stage-wise accuracy, verified recovery, penalized lifecycle latency, and token consumption. Across six agent-model configurations, faulty-state detection ranges from 72.7% to 90.9%, whereas overall recovery ranges from only 14.5% to 52.7%, exposing a substantial gap between recognizing incidents and resolving them end to end. Trajectory analysis further shows that reported diagnosis and final recovery only partially coincide: some tasks achieve verified recovery despite an incorrect reported RCA, while runtime symptom clearance can still fail fix-specific functional verification. SWEOps-Bench establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluating autonomous agents in integrated development and operational environments.

title: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks
summary: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain $0.0019$ MSE with $0.0038$ mean absolute bias at a low $\varepsilon$ of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of $0.0113$ MSE with $0.004$ mean absolute bias at $\varepsilon=2$.

title: SenTrojan: Revealing Analog Hardware Trojan Attacks on Sensors
summary: Sensors bridge the physical and digital worlds, making their integrity critical to cyber-physical system security. Existing sensor attacks largely exploit unintended and sensor-specific physical vulnerabilities, limiting their generalizability and motivating a different threat model, i.e., whether an adversary can implant hidden attack surfaces into sensors before deployment. In this paper, we present SenTrojan, an analog hardware Trojan framework for sensors. SenTrojan embeds malicious functionality into analog signal circuitry commonly shared across diverse sensor architectures, and activates the hidden behavior through crafted external physical signals. Once activated, SenTrojan can induce sensor malfunctions ranging from permanent denial-of-service to static or dynamic spoofing. To achieve these effects under different architectural constraints, we introduce two complementary designs. The Logic-Rule-Driven (LRD) Trojan adds lightweight analog monitoring logic to detect trigger features such as frequency and amplitude, enabling reliable activation across various sensor types. The Physical-Effect-Driven (PED) Trojan targets sensors with exploitable native analog effects, e.g., nonlinearity and rectification, and realizes attacks with minimal component insertion. We evaluate SenTrojan on 14 sensors spanning 6 transduction principles and demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse real-world scenarios. Overall, SenTrojan achieves an average successful trigger rate above 95%, maintains over 97% similarity to benign behavior, incurs zero false-trigger rate for LRD designs, and introduces less than 5% average deviation in drift, noise floor, and response time. To our knowledge, this work is the first systematic study of analog sensor Trojans, broadening sensor security from unintended physical vulnerabilities to intentional supply-chain compromise.

title: XuanJian-DINOSAR: A SAR Foundation Model Based on Global and Local Semantic Consistency
summary: Self-supervised pre-training on synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery enables transferable representations, but the optical-SAR domain gap and speckle perturbations limit representation stability. Most SAR foundation models use masked image modeling (MIM) through pixel reconstruction or structural feature prediction, which is sensitive to speckle or relies on predefined operators. Joint modeling of cross-view semantics and perturbation stability at corresponding spatial locations remains underexplored. We propose XuanJian-DINOSAR, a SAR foundation model based on global and local semantic consistency. We curate over 360K publicly available SAR target chips, detection images, and scene images spanning diverse targets, scenes, and sensors, and adapt an optically pre-trained DINOv2 model to SAR through self-supervised learning. The framework combines DINO global semantic self-distillation, iBOT local masked modeling, and KoLeo feature-distribution regularization to learn globally discriminative and locally structure-aware representations. We introduce a local semantic consistency branch tailored to SAR intensity statistics and coherent imaging characteristics. Shared geometric transformations produce spatially aligned teacher weak views and student strong views. Intensity transformations and Gamma multiplicative speckle perturbations are applied to student views, while a cosine consistency loss aligns patch tokens at corresponding locations, promoting stability under radiometric perturbations. This objective complements the cross-region and cross-scale semantic consistency of DINOv2 multi-crop training, jointly enforcing global and local semantic consistency. Experiments on multiple downstream classification and detection datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on most evaluation metrics, validating the generality and transferability of the learned representations.

title: Learning When to Think Aloud in Latent Reasoning
summary: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves efficiency by shifting intermediate computation into continuous hidden states. However, fully latent methods often struggle on precision-critical tasks such as mathematical reasoning, while existing hybrid approaches retain substantial token-generation overhead. We introduce VITAL, an importance-guided hybrid reasoning framework that selectively verbalizes informative tokens as reasoning anchors while keeping most computation latent. A lightweight gating head dynamically selects between explicit token generation and direct hidden-state feedback. VITAL constructs hybrid trajectories from explicit CoT using token- importance estimation and trains the model through curriculum-based supervised training, followed by reinforcement learning with a reward that balances correctness and conciseness. Experiments show that VITAL consistently out- performs existing fully latent reasoning methods, achieving relative average accuracy gains of 9.6% on GPT-2 and 5.1% on Llama-3.2-1B at comparable reasoning lengths. Compared with hybrid baselines, VITAL achieves higher reasoning accuracy with substantially shorter reasoning trajectories on Qwen3-1.7B.

title: Beyond Risk Cues: A Mechanism-Level Benchmark and Verifiable Debate for Scam Video Detection on the Web
summary: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.

title: Reconstruction and well-posedness of an inverse coefficient problem for a diffusion equation
summary: In this work, we investigate the inverse coefficient problem of determining an unknown coefficient in a diffusion equation from a single boundary flux measurement. More precisely, assuming that the domain is cylindrical, we develop a unified theoretical and numerical framework for the stable reconstruction of a space-time-dependent coefficient, by reformulating the inverse problem as a nonlinear equation. The inherent nonlinearity of the problem is transferred to an auxiliary nonlinear equation, enabling the application of techniques and concepts from nonlinear analysis. By combining representation formulas with regularity properties of solutions to diffusion equations, we extend to nonlinear inverse problems an approach that has so far been restricted to linear ones. The theoretical reconstruction procedure is complemented by a numerical analysis of the proposed method, including convergence and error estimates, as well as numerical experiments. The proposed reconstruction algorithm is directly inspired by the theoretical framework.

title: Semantic Prior-Guided Incomplete Cross-Modal Retrieval with Noisy Labels
summary: Cross-modal retrieval (CMR) aims to bridge the semantic gaps between modalities by learning shared representations. Unfortunately, due to the dynamism and inconsistencies in real-world data acquisition, multimodal datasets frequently encounter severe modality incompleteness. Existing incomplete CMR methods adhere to a label-driven paradigm, relying heavily on categorical annotations as the semantic benchmark. However, label noise is difficult to avoid and often coexists with modality incompleteness. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semantic prior-guided framework for incomplete cross-modal retrieval with noisy labels, termed SPIRN. Specifically, SPIRN uses fixed semantic priors as a consistent reference for robust representation learning, noisy-label handling, and missing-modality completion. Based on this reference, Semantic Priors Guidance (SPG) establishes a stable category-level semantic space, Quality-aware Robust Learning (QRL) dynamically evaluates sample quality to distinguish clean samples from noisy ones and handles noise via reverse learning, Prior-guided Global Label Calibration (PGLC) rectifies corrupted annotations for refined supervision, and Confidence-driven Selective Imputation (CSI) recovers missing modalities from a cross-modal memory bank while filtering unreliable imputations with an increasing threshold. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework to jointly tackle the dual challenges of modality incompleteness and label noise in the CMR community. Extensive experiments on four widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPIRN outperforms 11 state-of-the-art methods in various scenarios involving both missing modalities and noisy labels.

title: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models
comments: 16 pages, 4 tables. Pre-registered. Code, data and all 3120 episode traces: https://github.com/mhuyut/harness-is-the-model
summary: Banks validate language models, but they deploy systems: a model inside a harness that decides what it sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. We test whether that harness changes compliance with banking conduct rules when the model is held fixed. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a pipeline that makes one structured decision, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop in which the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose 11 rule families paraphrase EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. Every one of the 3120 two-turn episodes was scored deterministically from the executed tool trace, with violations and over-refusals counted separately. Pooled across models the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but within a model it mattered a great deal: for one model the spread between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last place among the four models, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the model x harness interaction itself was suggestive rather than conclusive. The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, contrary to our pre-registered prediction. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis with two LLM judges and a blind human check, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message that denied the action the agent had just executed, which a transcript-only review would record as a correct refusal. For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model-harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log, not the conversation.
comment: 16 pages, 4 tables. Pre-registered. Code, data and all 3120 episode traces: https://github.com/mhuyut/harness-is-the-model

title: Online Adaptation to Latent Physical Properties for Learning from Demonstration
comments: Accepted for the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
summary: Manipulating visually identical objects with different physical properties requires adapting actions based on information acquired through interaction. We address the problem of learning from demonstrations how to adapt manipulation actions, such as regrasping and changing contact locations, based on physical-property information acquired during interaction. To this end, we propose a learning-from-demonstration method that learns latent representations of physical properties needed to predict object responses and conditions a policy on online estimates of these representations. A dynamics model and object-specific latent representations are jointly learned from demonstrations that include behaviors adapting to the objects' physical properties, and the learned representations are then used to condition an imitation policy. During execution, the dynamics model and policy weights remain fixed, while the latent representation is updated based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual observations, allowing interaction with the object to inform action generation. Real-world and simulation experiments with objects whose centers of mass differ suggest that online adaptation through latent representations of physical properties can improve task success rates. However, in simulation, success rates on center-of-mass locations absent from the demonstrations remained around 30%, indicating limited adaptation to unseen physical properties. Project page: https://isri-aist.github.io/latent-dynamics-project-page/
comment: Accepted for the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)

title: ReactWorld: Structuring Interaction Responses for Embodied Video Generation
summary: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone's feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch's outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.

title: 3D Pose Estimation in Projection Space via Pixel-level Visible Light Communication
summary: Projector-based augmented reality enables natural interaction between users and devices by overlaying digital information onto the physical world through projected imagery. A key technical requirement of such systems is accurate positional alignment between the projector and the devices. Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC) achieves this alignment without external sensing infrastructure by embedding invisible spatial codes into each projected pixel through high-speed brightness modulation that preserves image quality. However, the information that PVLC transmits is inherently planar. PVLC has therefore been limited to devices moving on a flat surface and cannot estimate the 3D pose of devices in three-dimensional space, such as aerial robots. To extend PVLC-based pose estimation to three dimensions, we formulate it as a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem. The 2D pixel positions that four coplanar photosensors on the device receive via PVLC serve as the image points, and their known 3D layout provides the object points. Experiments show that the proposed system estimates 3D pose with a latency of approximately 8~ms and a 3D position RMSE of 19.2~mm after Kalman filtering. These results confirm the first realization of real-time 3D pose estimation coordinated with high-quality projected image content without external sensing infrastructure.

title: Ab Initio Accuracy Beyond the Cutoff: Distributed Message-Passing Equivariant Attention at Tens-of-Millions-of-Atom Scale
summary: Molecular dynamics predicts molecular motion from atomic forces and trajectory integration. Density functional theory (DFT) provides first-principles forces, but its $O(N^3)$ cost limits simulations to thousands of atoms; empirical force fields scale to millions but miss bond breaking and charge transfer. Equivariant message-passing Transformers learn the ab initio potential at linear cost. Stacked layers propagate information beyond a single cutoff, giving four layers a receptive field up to 23Å. At this frontier, scale is limited by communication: layers exchange boundary features across devices, force backpropagation repeats the exchange, and moving atoms change neighbor graphs and tensor shapes. We present Tessera, a distributed runtime that fixes workload shapes between rebuilds. It sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-count shards, ensuring identical atom counts and tensor shapes per rank. Peer sets scale as $K^{0.5}$, not $K$. A conservative neighbor skin preserves topology across updates, enabling each rebuild interval to replay as one CUDA Graph. Fused kernels, three-level neighbor search, and overlapped All-to-All complete it. On 512 GPUs, Tessera sustains 30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency (77--90% across three per-GPU loads); per-step time rises 1.11--1.29x as machine and problem grow 16x. Graph reuse cuts full-step time $1.87\times$. Across an $8\times$ device increase, neighbor-search cost grows $1.7\times$, versus $3.0\times$ for Morton order. In a live $10.24$M-atom salt solution, NVE energy drift is $0.42\,μ$eV/atom/ps over $10$ ps, and structure matches a serial reference. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid sustains 100 ps of NVT at $\approx 8$ ps/day on 256 A100 GPUs. Over 200,000 steps, it has no broken bonds or anomalously close pairs and uses three compiled variants, with no graph breaks or eager fallbacks.

title: From Handcrafted to Generative: RLVR-Optimized Icon Generation for Alexa+
summary: Alexa+ devices with screens display animated icons during conversations to visually reinforce what is being said. The original set of these icons was hand-drawn by designers one at a time, a process that produces polished results but is time-consuming and cannot scale to the range of topics encountered in open-ended conversation. We describe an automated pipeline, deployed in production, that generates these vectorised animated icons from a text description alone and surfaces relevant animations to customers based on their ongoing conversation. The pipeline decomposes icon creation into a sequence of stages (image generation, semantic decomposition, vectorisation, styling, and animation). Its quality is determined at the very first of these, image generation, on which every downstream stage depends. We therefore focus on improving this first and most critical stage. Because the icons are rendered on small display canvases under strict design guidelines, generations are often unsuitable for production. Supervised fine-tuning is not viable, as no dataset of line-art icons exists under these constraints. Instead, we design objective verifiers that automatically flag generations violating the design guidelines, and use them to fine-tune a flow matching image generation model via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The fine-tuned model raises the pass rate from 15.7% to 58.7% (3.7x) under a VLM judge that is independent of the reward model. Both the trained model and the verifier are deployed in the production pipeline, where the verifier also serves as the automated quality gate before final design review.

title: NN-Based FeFET Compact Modeling for SPICE Simulation
summary: Prototyping and early-stage circuit evaluation for emerging transistor technologies require fast and accurate compact models for SPICE simulations. Standard physics-based compact models, such as BSIM, offer high fidelity but demand extensive domain expertise and time-consuming equation formulation for every new physical effect, significantly slowing technology development. Neural network (NN)-based models offer a scalable alternative approach, but they rely heavily on smooth numerical solver data with explicit high-order derivative information. However, measurement data suffers from complex noise patterns, making derivative extraction challenging and complicating NN-based transistor modeling. This work presents a derivative-free NN training framework employing spectral normalization to naturally smooth derivative behavior and filter measurement noise. Using drain current measurements from a fabricated 28 nm ferroelectric device, we design an NN-based compact model that captures the full spectrum of polarization amplitudes and supports dynamic polarization switching in transient simulations. To demonstrate its capability, we deploy the model in a commercial SPICE software to simulate write and read operations for large-scale memory arrays with up to 512x512 size, including parasitic effects. Our approach bridges raw measurements with NN-based SPICE-compatible transistor modeling, significantly reducing model development time and enabling rapid circuit-level prototyping for emerging devices.

title: Short-Term Forecasting of Heterogeneous Wind Power Fleets: Global Temporal Fusion Transformer Leveraging Static Covariates
comments: 18th International Green Energy Conference (IGEC-XVIII) & the 7th International Conference on Energy and AI (ICEAI-VII)
summary: Accurate short-term wind power forecasting is critical for grid stability and electricity trading. While transformer-based deep learning is state of the art, industry practice relies mostly on local models trained for individual assets. This study investigates whether a global temporal fusion transformer (TFT), trained jointly on a heterogeneous portfolio of wind farms across Germany, outperforms site-specific local models in 48-hour-ahead forecasting. Using numerical weather prediction (NWP) data from the regional ICON-D2 and the global ECMWF HRES models, we compare the global TFT against local models and a linear regression baseline. The global model leverages static covariates, such as farm age, altitude above sea level, hub height, rotor diameter and power curve parameters, to learn shared representations across sites. We evaluate on 100 synthetic wind farm profiles and a real portfolio of 11 German wind farms, across two seasonal test periods with intermediate retraining. The global TFT outperforms the local models for 87% of the synthetic and 77% of the real wind farms and clearly surpasses the linear baseline. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm that these gains are significant across both seasons and datasets. Crucially, this superiority depends on static covariates: without asset-specific context, the global model fails to generalize. The TFT's variable selection network (VSN) reveals the learned feature selection. Altitude emerges as a relevant static discriminator on both datasets, while hub height is decisive on the real portfolio. For dynamic inputs, the encoder prioritizes historical power, whereas the decoder combines upper-level wind speeds from both NWP models, consistent with averaging out model-specific errors. These findings support a shift from single-site to scalable multi-site forecasting, reducing operational complexity while improving accuracy in large portfolios.
comment: 18th International Green Energy Conference (IGEC-XVIII) & the 7th International Conference on Energy and AI (ICEAI-VII)

title: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search
summary: Static and incomplete parametric knowledge limits the performance of multimodal large language models on novel-knowledge and knowledge-intensive tasks, especially those requiring multi-hop evidence acquisition. Existing multimodal agentic search methods often fix visual evidence at the input or a predefined trajectory position, making it difficult for agents to select search modalities as their information needs evolve and to handle complex real-world queries. We define this capability as autonomous cross-modal search: an agent chooses among direct reasoning, text-to-text search, text-to-image search, and reverse-image search, actively introduces visual evidence when appropriate, and switches between and integrates modalities across multiple hops. We propose ModalSearch-Pipeline, a scalable procedure for constructing an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph. It samples paths with diverse depths and modality compositions and uses backward question construction to obscure entity names and image targets that would expose reasoning shortcuts while retaining necessary disambiguating clues, yielding text-only, image-initialized, and arbitrarily interleaved multi-hop problems. We train the ModalSearcher Agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and construct ModalSearch-Bench. Experiments show that ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.

title: Growing One's AI Tools: A Paradigm of Practice-Grown Tools
summary: Professionals have long used software built for them by others. This article reports the growth of a professional computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tool built by its own user, a conference interpreter without programming training. Drawing on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, the article traces how real conference work drove the tool through 62 commits and six versions. The record shows capabilities deployed on the day their need appeared and one strategy change that cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon. The article then proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools, defined by the shift from using to growing, the co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary, and it formulates three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what they and their tools achieve together.

title: Accelerating Long-Context Decoding in Large-Scale Hybrid LLMs Without Retraining
comments: 19 pages (main body: 10 pages, references: 3 pages, appendix: 6 pages), 8 figures, 6 tables
summary: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
comment: 19 pages (main body: 10 pages, references: 3 pages, appendix: 6 pages), 8 figures, 6 tables

title: SBVUL: Statement-Based Vulnerability Detection
summary: Many recent approaches for vulnerability detection use large language models (LLMs) to classify functions as vulnerable or benign, leaving developers to locate the exploitable statements. Furthermore, while these approaches have shown performance improvements, they still fall short in distinguishing vulnerable from patched real-world functions. This paper presents SBVul, an agentic approach that detects exploitable statements in C/C++ functions. In Phase~1, an LLM agent explores the function and its repository and identifies candidate statements. In Phase~2, a second agent analyzes the control and data flow of each candidate and confirms it, rules it out, or marks it uncertain. We created a manually verified ground truth of exploitable statements for 200 pairs of the PrimeVul Paired test set and ran SBVul with the open-weight models Qwen 3.8 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. Phase~1 identifies ground-truth statements in 56--77% of the vulnerable functions, and Phase~2 confirms such a statement with an explanation accepted by an LLM judge in 26--73%. However, all models also confirm candidates in 23--61% of the patched functions. Across vulnerable and patched functions, the highest statement-level precision is 0.315 at a recall of 0.605 obtained with Opus 5.5 (xhigh). At the function level, SBVul with Opus 5.5 classifies 42.0% of the pairs correctly, compared with 33.8% reported for the best previous approach.

title: Essential Unitarity for Higher-Order Quantum Computation (Extended Abstract)
summary:
We develop a boundary-centric semantic framework for higher-order quantum computation, building on the Kelly-Laplaza description of compact closure and Abramsky's execution account. In the semantic carrier Perm(C), morphisms are complex-linear combinations of polarized boundary linkings, composed by execution. Finite-family addresses provide coherent control over finite-level quantum registers (qudits) while retaining the multiplicative boundary structure.
  We identify essential unitarity, a boundary condition extending ordinary unitarity to higher-order interfaces. On positive qudit registers it coincides with ordinary matrix unitarity; at higher order it expresses preservation of information across the full polarized boundary.
  We define a unit-free coherent quantum core generated bymultiplicative wiring, unitary gates on positive qudit registers, and contextual coherent control, and prove that every one of its morphisms is essentially unitary. The framework realizes an applied coherent quantum switch and the unitary stages of equal-ratio one-slot supermap dilations with explicit memory. Complete proofs appear in the full version of this paper.

title: KVGuard: A KV Cache Safety Checker for LLM Serving Systems
summary: Modern LLM serving systems manage the KV cache through PagedAttention, a custom GPU allocator that partitions a single CUDA-allocated region into fixed-size physical blocks and maps each request to those blocks through a CPU-built block table. This block-based design exposes a previously unstudied class of memory safety bugs in the KV cache, including double-free, use-after-free, out-of-bounds access, uninitialized read, and permission violation, which silently corrupt outputs or break request isolation without ever crashing the system. Existing memory sanitizers cannot detect them, because they reason about CUDA-level addresses rather than KV cache blocks, requests, and block tables, and their redzone- and quarantine-based designs do not fit the scarce GPU memory budget of LLM serving. This paper presents KVGuard, the first systematic memory-safety abstraction for KV cache management in LLM serving systems. KVGuard maintains a compact shadow block for each physical KV block, recording per-request permission and per-entry initialization, and uses this metadata to perform five safety checks across the PagedAttention workflow, spanning CPU allocation, block table construction and translation, and GPU-side block table lookup and KV entry access. Each check fires at the boundary that introduced the violation, enabling early detection during development rather than reporting downstream output corruption many requests later. A prototype of KVGuard on vLLM and SGLang covers all 29 historical real-world KV cache safety bugs collected from the two systems' patch histories. KVGuard further found 8 previously unknown safety violations while reporting no false positives. It adds 3.0% and 7.4% geomean TPOT overhead on Qwen 2.5 14B on vLLM and SGLang and at most 0.11% of the KV cache in memory overhead, two orders of magnitude below NVIDIA Compute Sanitizer on the same workloads.

title: Pauli Gadget Synthesis for Gatesets with Arbitrary Even Arity Clifford Gates
summary:
We propose an algorithm that can synthesize circuits to gate sets consisting of a 2n-arity Clifford gate and arbitrary single qubit rotations. To do this, we represent the circuit as a sequence of Pauli gadgets and jointly synthesize them by placing the multi-qubit Clifford in the synthesized circuit and pushing its adjoint through the remaining gadgets such that some qubits are disconnected from some gadgets. The pushed gadgets are collected in a Clifford tableau, which is decomposed afterwards.
  With the help of our algorithm we run experiments where we synthesize circuits to varying sizes of target multi-qubit gates. These experiments indicate that increases in gate size can lead to smaller output circuits, and that different connectivity constraints have meaningful differences in how higher arity gates effect the circuit sized.

title: RDT-3D: Resolution-Decoupled Training for High-Fidelity 3D Geometry Generation
summary: High-fidelity 3D geometry generation requires maintaining global structural coherence alongside fine-grained surface details. While recent coarse-to-fine frameworks leverage Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to condition local queries, we reveal a critical training-inference resolution discrepancy: coordinate guidance and geometric supervision are aligned during training, whereas inference decodes high-resolution geometry from coarse spatial coordinates. This mismatch introduces a severe distribution shift that degrades fine details. To overcome this, we propose Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT), which anchors RoPE guidance at 512 resolution while supervising geometry at 1536, enabling robust detail extrapolation. Additionally, to eliminate high-resolution data bottlenecks, we present Dual3D-300K, a large-scale paired dataset comprising 300K watertight 3D point clouds explicitly aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RDT substantially improves sharp geometric regions, while Dual3D-300K offers a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.

title: PTQ4SAM3: Semantics-Preserving Post-Training Quantization for Segment Anything Model 3
comments: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to WACV 2027. Includes supplementary material
summary: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) can segment objects from text prompts and track them across video, but its memory and computation costs make deployment difficult. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by using fewer bits. However, a quantized model can select the wrong object or lose track of its target across frames. We call this prompt-alignment drift. Controlled tests show that perturbing low-variance feature directions strongly affects target selection. We propose Semantics-Preserving Quantization (SPQ), which gives more calibration weight to concept-sensitive parameters, preserves residual features, and corrects the mean error in video memory. Fixed text concepts guide calibration without task annotations. All three components operate offline and add no inference operators. With a W4A8 image encoder, SPQ improves RefCOCO Pr@0.5 from 42.1 to 72.5 over PTQ4SAM while retaining 54.8 COCO mask AP. Experiments on LVIS, RefCOCO variants, and SA-V show consistent gains. A CLIP study also shows improved image-text retrieval.
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to WACV 2027. Includes supplementary material

title: Analyzing Simultaneous Charging Factors of Electric Vehicles Using Monte Carlo Simulation: A Case Study in Phu Quoc City, Vietnam
comments: 11 pages, 17 figures. Accepted for publication in GMSARN International Journal (expected in Issue 3, 2027). Author-prepared accepted manuscript
summary: This study estimates the simultaneous charging factor (SCF) of electric vehicles (EVs) in Phu Quoc City, Vietnam, using a Monte Carlo simulation. Three planning scenarios (2030, 2035, and 2040) are developed from population-based EV uptake assumptions and vehicle-specific charging probability profiles over 24 hours, reflecting distinct operating patterns of motorbikes, cars, taxis, and buses. For each vehicle class and scenario, 1,000 simulation runs are performed to compute SCF and its uncertainty, reported via 95% confidence intervals. Results indicate that SCF decreases as EV penetration increases, implying more temporally dispersed charging demand and a reduced likelihood of extreme coincidence. For electric buses, SCF declines from 0.76 (2030) to 0.59 (2040), and other vehicle groups show similarly decreasing trends across the horizon. These SCF estimates provide practical inputs for grid-aware charging infrastructure planning, including diversity factors for sizing distribution transformers and feeders, identifying peak-hour stress, and informing demand management measures such as time of use tariffs and basic smart charging controls.
comment: 11 pages, 17 figures. Accepted for publication in GMSARN International Journal (expected in Issue 3, 2027). Author-prepared accepted manuscript

title: Multi-Period Bilevel Coordination of Primary and Secondary Frequency Regulation for Grid-Forming Battery Energy Storage
summary: We study the coordination of primary and secondary frequency regulation by grid-forming battery energy storage systems in islanded microgrids. We formulate the coordination as a multi-period bilevel program, in which the upper level schedules secondary regulation setpoints and each lower level computes primary regulation decisions. Using the lower-level Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, we obtain an exact single-level reformulation with complementarity constraints. To address the numerical difficulties introduced by these constraints, we develop a continuation method that couples the complementarity relaxation parameter with the interior-point barrier parameter and warm-starts successive stages. Under the stated boundedness assumptions and with vanishing subproblem residuals, we prove that every accumulation point is feasible and satisfies a first-order stationarity condition for the reformulated problem (C-stationarity). Numerical results for an islanded microgrid show that the proposed method reduces solution time by 89.3% and peak frequency deviation by 0.53% relative to conventional Scholtes relaxation.

title: SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.

title: Grounding in the Dark: Text-Only Training for Zero-Shot Video Temporal Localization
summary: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points.
